cases.refreshed: This program is best for children ages 2-8 with their caregivers, but all children with caregivers are welcome. Join us every Wednesday for Music and Movement at the King Library Children's Room! Music and Movement is designed to accommodate a mix of ages; we invite the entire family to participate in early literacy activities and develop motor skills through song and movement activities - sometimes with scarves, shaky eggs, and rhythm sticks! Music and Movement is a high energy Storytime - a fun and interactive experience for the whole family that promotes the joys of learning and movement. We'll start with a story, then move and groove to our monthly playlist. Free, with limited capacity. Program finishes by 6:10 PM. This program is developed to align with the Early Education Quality Standards.

events.title: Playdates for Children and Their Caregivers

cases.refreshed: Join us every Wednesday for weekly playdates. Kids get to practice early social skills like sharing, taking turns, imitation of play, and joint attention while caregivers get a chance to connect. Don't miss out on this chance to celebrate the joys of play while connecting with other families in the community. It's a wonderful way to learn through play and create lasting memories together! 1st Wednesday: Cars 2nd Wednesday: Superhero Obstacle Course (ages 3-8) 3rd Wednesday: LEGO Duplo Blocks 4th Wednesday: Cars 5th Wednesday: LEGO Duplo Blocks Recommended for children ages 2 – 6 years old.

cases.refreshed: Our nonverbal communication plays a critical role in our workplace and personal interactions. However, we rarely pause and reflect about how we are presenting ourselves through our tone and body language. This workshop will help you manage your nonverbal communication to have more successful interactions in the workplace and in your personal life. This programs is immediately proceeded by: Putting your best face forward: Managing interview questions through the STAR method In partnership with SJSU Department of Communication Studies Free. cases.refreshed: Middle and high schoolers: Come explore the TeenHQ Maker Space! Up to 5 teens at a time can use the space to utilize our 3D printers, Poster Printer, Glow Forge, Sewing & Serger Machines, Cricut, Button Press, and miscellaneous craft supplies. Work with our teen librarian to bring your idea to life. Each machine and other materials have limitations and time requirements. Pre-registration is recommended to reserve your spot. If not all claimed registration spots have arrived by 4:30 PM, they will be given to those waiting. All services are provided for free to middle and high school (6-12 grade) students. Younger people and adults are not permitted in the area unless required to assist with a disability. Pre-registration will start 1 week before the start of the program. Please un-register yourself if you find you're unable to attend at a later date. Registration closes 1 hour before the start of the program. There will not be a waitlist for pre-registration. Drop-ins will be accepted if not all registration slots are filled and if not all registered individuals arrive by 4:30 PM. The area is wheelchair accessible from the Children's Room elevator. Other accommodations can be made available with request. Please note that each device requires time to set up, use, and complete whatever task you're wanting to use the space for. Be sure that you have enough time in your schedule to attend the program. Not all tasks may be completed before the end of the program and you may need to return to get your completed items or pause your task and restart at another studio session. We appreciate your patience and flexibility. 3D Printing: All requested prints must take less than 4.5 hours to print. All requested prints will need to be picked up at a later date. Contact information is required for notification of pick-up. 3D print quality and time needed to complete prints is not guaranteed. Multiple objects can be printed as long as the total time does not exceed 4.5 hours. Poster Printing: All prints must be assembled on a 2"x3" canvas and printed as a. Png. Please see the regularly scheduled poster printing event for further details. One poster per teen per day. Glow Forge: Create a custom engraved object. Object should follow similar guidelines to the Custom Keychain Program. Complexity of request is at the discretion of the librarian. Sewing & Serger Machines: It is recommended that you bring your own fabric and thread if fabric is special or color is a factor. There are scrap material and thread available but we cannot guarantee material quality or availability. An iron and ironing board is also available. Cricut: Basic Cricut supplies are available, such as construction and cardstock paper. If your project is specialized, such as requiring iron-on, you'll need to bring your own materials. It is recommended that you know the requirements for any materials you provide. Button Press: TeenHQ offers two sizes of button presses. We cannot offer printing. If your bring your own printout of buttons, it must be printed on standard printer paper. Paper thicker than standard printer paper cannot be used on the button presses. All measurements below are diameter length in inches. Small Button Press: 1.25" Large Button Press: 2.25" Picture Size: 1.156" Cut Line: 1.629" Picture Size: 2.063" Cut Line: 2.625"

cases.refreshed: Monthly book discussion on a graphic novel selected by the group! This program is for readers age 16 and up. 2026-2027 titles: September 10 - Ginseng Roots: A Memoir by Craig Thompson (2025) 448 pages. Nonfiction. USA; October 8 - The Winter of the Cartoonist by Paco Roca (author) and Andrea Rosenberg (translator) (2020) 128 pages. Historical nonfiction. Spain. Translation; November 12 - It's Not What You Thought It Would Be by Lizzy Stewart (2021) 168 pages. Fiction. Coming-of-age story of young women. The author, originally from Scotland, lives in London, England. December 10 - Impossible People: A Completely Average Recovery Story by Julia Wertz (2023) 320 pages. Nonfiction. Julia Wertz lives in Sonoma County; January 14 - Love Languages by James Albon (2025) 176 pages. Queer romance graphic novel set in France. Fiction. James Albon is from Scotland. February 11 - Illegal: A Graphic Novel by Eoin Colfer (Author), Andrew Donkin (Author), Giovanni Rigano (Illustrator) (2018) 144 pages. Fiction, based on real events. It explores the current plight of undocumented immigrants. March 11 - More Weight: A Salem Story by Ben Wickey (2025) 532 pages. Historical nonfiction. The book explores the infamous Salem witch trials and the long shadows they cast more than 300 years later. USA; April 8 - The Waiting by Keum Suk Gendry-Kim (2021) 247 pages. Fiction, based on real events. Story of a Korean family separated by the war. Translation. May 13 - You and a Bike and a Road by Eleanor Davis (2024) 172 pages. Nonfiction. A two-wheeled journey across the landscape of America, and through the heart and mind of an artist. USA. Titles can be borrowed from the Palo Alto City Library and through our Link+ system - click on the links above or search in our catalog for more information. Meetings are held in person in the Midtown Room at Mitchell Park Library and facilitated by Danièle Archambault. Danièle Archambault, Ph. D. (Linguistics), is a researcher, author, and educator who is interested in comics as a way to document a society's cultural and linguistic landscape. Originally from Montreal, Quebec, she now lives in Palo Alto, where she is an artist in residence at the Cubberley Artist Studio Program, a program of the City of Palo Alto. In the past few years, she has published several full-color comic books, graphic novels, and electronic books. Ms. Archambault is a regular guest speaker on documenting culture and dialects through comics at various educational and cultural institutions. She teaches Visual Storytelling at the Palo Alto Art Center, and at other educational venues. http://danielebd.com/
